slots.practicalActivity: In the Azure portal, create a real Storage Account and enable the Hierarchical namespace option to make it ADLS Gen2, then create a second account with Hierarchical namespace left disabled and compare the two side by side in the portal's Containers / Data Lake Storage Gen2 blades.
slots.deliverable: Two real Storage Accounts (one Blob, one ADLS Gen2), with a written note on which portal settings differ between them.

slots.practicalActivity: In your ADLS Gen2 account, create a container named taxi-data with nested directories (raw/, cleansed/, curated/), then use Storage Explorer or the portal's Storage browser to confirm the hierarchical namespace lets you rename or move a directory in one atomic operation rather than rewriting every blob's key.
slots.deliverable: A taxi-data container with a real raw/cleansed/curated directory structure, and a note confirming an atomic directory rename actually worked.

slots.practicalActivity: On your ADLS Gen2 account, assign yourself the Storage Blob Data Contributor RBAC role at the container level, then set a POSIX ACL on one specific subdirectory that restricts access further, and write a short note on which control actually wins in a conflict.
slots.deliverable: One RBAC role assignment and one ACL entry on the same storage account, with a written note explaining which one takes precedence for a given operation.

lessons.title: CSV vs. JSON vs. Parquet vs. Delta

slots.practicalActivity: Generate a time-limited SAS token scoped to just the raw/ directory and use it to upload a small NYC Taxi CSV file without using your full account key, then write the same sample data out as CSV, JSON, and Parquet locally and compare file sizes.
slots.deliverable: One file uploaded via a scoped SAS token, plus a 3-way file-size comparison (CSV/JSON/Parquet) of the same sample data.

slots.practicalActivity: Partition a sample of NYC Taxi data into year=/month= folder partitions inside your raw/ directory, then sketch a full data lake design — zones, partitioning scheme, and file format per zone — for the complete NYC Taxi dataset going back to 2009.
slots.deliverable: A partitioned sample upload (e.g. year=2024/month=01/...) plus a written data lake design document covering zones, partitioning, and format choices.

slots.practicalActivity: Relabel your raw/cleansed/curated directory structure with bronze/silver/gold naming (as a documented equivalence), and write the one-paragraph explanation of the one real difference between the two namings — Delta tables vs. plain files — that this lesson teaches.
slots.deliverable: A written bronze/silver/gold-to-raw/cleansed/curated equivalence note that explicitly names the one real, non-vocabulary difference.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter 1 capstone lab: provision (or reuse) a real ADLS Gen2 account with raw/cleansed/curated containers, upload a real NYC Taxi monthly trip CSV into the raw zone partitioned by year/month, assign RBAC at the container level, and generate a SAS token for read-only access to the curated zone.
slots.deliverable: A fully structured ADLS Gen2 account — 3 zones, partitioned raw data, RBAC assigned, one scoped SAS token issued — ready for Chapter 2's Python to read from.

slots.practicalActivity: Set up a local Python environment (or a notebook) and write a short script declaring variables for a real data-pipeline configuration — file paths, table names, row-count thresholds — using the correct Python data type for each one.
slots.deliverable: One Python script with at least 6 well-typed variables representing real data-pipeline configuration values.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a Python list of NYC Taxi column names and a dictionary mapping each column to its expected data type, then write conditional logic that checks whether a sample row's values match the expected types, printing a pass/fail message per column.
slots.deliverable: A script using a list and a dictionary to validate one sample row's column types, with conditional pass/fail output printed.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a function that validates a single NYC Taxi row against the previous slot's type rules, then use a loop to call it against every row in a small sample CSV, counting how many rows pass and how many fail.
slots.deliverable: One validation function called in a loop across a sample dataset, printing total pass/fail counts.

slots.practicalActivity: Wrap your file-reading code in try/except blocks that handle a missing file and a malformed row gracefully, then write a script that opens, reads, and closes a real NYC Taxi CSV file using a with open(...) context manager.
slots.deliverable: A script that handles a deliberately-missing file and a malformed row without crashing, using proper file-handling syntax.

slots.practicalActivity: Load a real NYC Taxi CSV into a Pandas DataFrame with pd.read_csv, and load a sample JSON file (e.g. a taxi zone lookup) with pd.read_json or json.load, inspecting both with .head() and .dtypes.
slots.deliverable: Two DataFrames — one from CSV, one from JSON — with .head() and .dtypes output captured for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Call a free public REST API (e.g. a weather or holiday API) with the requests library, parse the JSON response, and flatten a nested field into a usable Python dictionary or DataFrame row, framing it as enrichment data you could join onto the taxi dataset by date.
slots.deliverable: A working REST API call with its nested JSON response flattened into usable Python data.

slots.practicalActivity: Connect Python to a real SQL Server instance (pyodbc or sqlalchemy against a local database) and run a query pulling a small table into a DataFrame, then apply at least 3 cleaning operations — dropna, invalid-value filtering, deduplication — to a sample of NYC Taxi data.
slots.deliverable: One Python-to-SQL query result loaded into a DataFrame, plus a cleaned NYC Taxi DataFrame with at least 3 documented cleaning steps applied.

lessons.title: Building a Simple Python ETL Process

slots.practicalActivity: Build your own version of this lesson's extract/transform/load ETL script — using a different NYC Taxi file or a different set of validation rules than the lesson's example — writing the cleansed result to Parquet in your Chapter 1 cleansed/ zone.
slots.deliverable: One original Python ETL script (extract/transform/load functions, wrapped in try/except) writing a cleaned Parquet file into the ADLS Gen2 cleansed zone.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter 2 lab: extend your ETL script to also call a REST API for enrichment data and merge it into the taxi DataFrame before writing the final Parquet output, with full try/except error handling around both the API call and the file I/O.
slots.deliverable: One extended ETL script combining file-based extraction, REST API enrichment, cleaning, and a Parquet load step, run successfully end to end.

slots.practicalActivity: Try loading a deliberately oversized concatenation of several months of NYC Taxi CSVs into Pandas on your own machine (or reason through the memory math if you don't have enough RAM to actually try it) to directly observe Pandas' single-machine ceiling, then write a short explanation of how a distributed cluster would instead split that same workload across multiple machines.
slots.deliverable: A written note (with a real or reasoned-through demonstration) explaining exactly where and why Pandas breaks down on a dataset too large for one machine.

slots.practicalActivity: Sign into Databricks Community Edition (or a local Spark install) and create a cluster, then inspect the Spark UI to identify the driver and each executor, noting how many cores and executors your cluster has available.
slots.deliverable: A running Spark cluster with a Spark UI note identifying the driver and its executors.

slots.practicalActivity: Load a sample NYC Taxi file into a Spark DataFrame on your cluster and check its default partition count with .rdd.getNumPartitions(), then explain in writing how that partition count relates to how many nodes or cores can work on the data in parallel.
slots.deliverable: One Spark DataFrame load with its partition count printed, plus a written note connecting partition count to parallelism.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a chain of Spark transformations (filter, select, withColumn) against your taxi DataFrame without calling any action and confirm nothing actually runs yet, then call .count() and .show() as actions and observe exactly when execution triggers.
slots.deliverable: One transformation chain with no action called (confirmed nothing executes), followed by the same chain triggered by .count() and .show().

slots.practicalActivity: Create a SparkSession explicitly (rather than relying on a pre-created one), use it to read your NYC Taxi CSV into a Spark DataFrame with .read.csv(), and inspect its schema with .printSchema().
slots.deliverable: One explicitly-created SparkSession reading a real taxi file into a Spark DataFrame with its schema printed.

slots.practicalActivity: Register your Spark DataFrame as a temporary view and write 3 Spark SQL queries against it — a filter, an aggregate, and a sort — comparing each SQL query's result against the equivalent DataFrame API call.
slots.deliverable: 3 working Spark SQL queries against a registered temp view, each with its DataFrame-API equivalent noted alongside it.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter 3 wrap: set up (or confirm) a working Spark environment, load real NYC Taxi data into a Spark DataFrame via an explicit SparkSession, and run both a lazy transformation chain and a Spark SQL query against it, writing a one-paragraph recap of how driver/executor/partition concepts applied to what you just ran.
slots.deliverable: One end-to-end Spark session (load, transform, SQL query) plus a written recap connecting it to this chapter's architecture concepts.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a small PySpark DataFrame by hand from a Python list of rows to understand the API without a file, then read a real NYC Taxi CSV file with spark.read.csv(..., header=True, inferSchema=True).
slots.deliverable: One manually-created DataFrame and one real CSV-loaded DataFrame, both displayed with .show().

slots.practicalActivity: Read a taxi zone lookup file in JSON format and the same data saved as Parquet with spark.read.json() and spark.read.parquet(), comparing the inferred schemas between the two formats.
slots.deliverable: The same lookup dataset loaded from both JSON and Parquet, with schema differences noted.

slots.practicalActivity: Define an explicit StructType schema for the NYC Taxi columns (instead of relying on inferSchema) and re-read the CSV with it applied, then use .select() to pull out 5 specific columns into a new DataFrame.
slots.deliverable: One explicitly-schema'd DataFrame load, plus a .select() call producing a 5-column subset.

slots.practicalActivity: Filter the taxi DataFrame to exclude zero or negative fare_amount and trip_distance rows using both .filter() and .where() syntax, then use .withColumn() to add a computed fare_per_mile column.
slots.deliverable: A filtered DataFrame (both filter/where syntax demonstrated) with a new fare_per_mile computed column.

slots.practicalActivity: Use when()/otherwise() to bucket trips into short, medium, and long based on trip_distance, then use .cast() to convert a string-typed fare column to a proper numeric type if your source file loaded it as text.
slots.deliverable: One when()-based trip-length bucket column and one explicit type-cast conversion, both verified with .show().

slots.practicalActivity: Use PySpark string functions (upper(), trim(), substring()) to clean a text column, and date functions (year(), month(), datediff()) to extract pickup year/month and compute trip duration from the pickup and dropoff timestamps.
slots.deliverable: A DataFrame with cleaned string columns and derived year/month/trip-duration date columns.

slots.practicalActivity: Use .na.drop() and .na.fill() to handle nulls in passenger_count two different ways (dropping vs. filling with a default), then use .dropDuplicates() to remove exact-duplicate rows, comparing row counts before and after each operation.
slots.deliverable: Before/after row counts for null-dropping, null-filling, and deduplication, each run as a separate step.

slots.practicalActivity: Use .groupBy("PULocationID") with .agg() to compute total trips, average fare, and average distance per pickup location, sorting the result by total trips descending.
slots.deliverable: One grouped aggregation DataFrame ranking pickup locations by trip count, average fare, and average distance.

slots.practicalActivity: Join your taxi DataFrame to a taxi zone lookup table on PULocationID/LocationID to bring in real borough and zone names, then .union() two different months' taxi DataFrames together into one combined DataFrame.
slots.deliverable: One joined DataFrame with real zone names attached, plus one unioned multi-month DataFrame with a correct combined row count.

slots.practicalActivity: Use a window function (Window.partitionBy("PULocationID").orderBy(...)) with rank() or row_number() to find each pickup location's highest-fare trip, then register the result as a temporary view and query it with Spark SQL.
slots.deliverable: One window-function ranking query (top trip per pickup location) exposed as a queryable temp view.

slots.practicalActivity: Mix Spark SQL and DataFrame API calls in a single pipeline (e.g. a SQL query feeding into a DataFrame .filter()), then write the final result with .write.mode("overwrite").parquet(...) into your Chapter 1 curated zone.
slots.deliverable: One mixed SQL/DataFrame pipeline with its output written as Parquet into the ADLS Gen2 curated zone.

slots.practicalActivity: Write your final output partitioned by pickup_year/pickup_month with .partitionBy(), then apply .cache() before running multiple actions against the same cleaned DataFrame, and use a broadcast() join against the small zone lookup table, comparing the join's plan with and without the broadcast hint.
slots.deliverable: One partitioned Parquet write plus a cached DataFrame with a broadcast-join comparison (with and without broadcast()) documented.

slots.practicalActivity: Mid-chapter lab: build one PySpark script covering DataFrame creation through null/duplicate handling end to end against a full real NYC Taxi monthly file — load, apply an explicit schema, filter, add computed columns, clean strings/dates, and handle nulls and duplicates — without looking back at individual lesson examples.
slots.deliverable: One original PySpark cleaning script combining schema definition, filtering, column derivation, and null/duplicate handling, run successfully against a real taxi file.

slots.practicalActivity: Course capstone lab: build the full pipeline the final PySpark lesson describes as one complete script — filter and cache the cleaned taxi DataFrame, broadcast-join it against the zone lookup table, rank trips per zone with a window function, and write the final result partitioned by pickup year/month to Parquet.
slots.deliverable: One complete, original PySpark pipeline (filter, cache, broadcast join, window ranking, partitioned Parquet write) run successfully end to end.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short course-completion reflection connecting all 4 chapters: point to the specific ADLS Gen2 zone structure (Chapter 1), the Python ETL script (Chapter 2), the Spark architecture concepts (Chapter 3), and the final PySpark pipeline (Chapter 4) you built, and note 2 specific things you expect to need from the next course, Azure Databricks & Delta Lake, to turn these Parquet outputs into managed Delta tables.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written course reflection tying together your Chapter 1-4 artifacts, plus 2 specific open questions carried forward into the Azure Databricks & Delta Lake course.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can structure a real Azure data lake into secured, zoned storage, write a working Python ETL script, and build real PySpark pipelines against the NYC Taxi dataset — reading, cleaning, joining, aggregating, and writing partitioned Parquet output — the foundation the rest of the Azure/Fabric Data Engineer path builds on.
